title: 2026 National Hybrid Schools Survey Report
author: Eric Wearne
summary: Eric Wearne of the National Hybrid Schools Project summarizes the fifth annual National Hybrid Schools Survey, a descriptive census of a sector that includes private schools, charter schools, public school programs and homeschool groups and appears in no other single dataset. He highlights three sections. Tuition averaged $6,359 with a median of $5,548, which sits below average ESA, tax-credit and voucher award amounts, so the model is within reach of most school choice funding. Schools that responded in multiple years show average enrollment growth, suggesting both more hybrid schools and more students enrolled in them. Finally he previews spinoff studies on AI attitudes, teacher hiring and how leaders define success, where religious observance mattered more than test scores or college matriculation. He cautions that the sample changes yearly, so numeric changes across surveys should be read carefully.
points: Reported hybrid school tuition averaged about $6,400, below typical ESA and voucher amounts, so funding programs can cover most of it.
Because the sample shifts each year, the most reliable evidence of growth comes from schools that responded repeatedly.
Repeat responders show positive average enrollment change, which suggests growth within existing schools as well as in the number of schools.
Hybrid leaders favored tightly regulated student-facing AI and were more enthusiastic about AI than teachers and parents, who were more skeptical.
When defining success, hybrid leaders weighed religious observance, civic life and family outcomes more heavily than testing or college matriculation.
quotes: These schools do not exist as a group in any other single dataset, as the field includes private schools, charter schools, conventional public school programs, and groups of homeschoolers.
Our responding schools this year reported a mean tuition of $6,359 and median tuition of $5,548.
But it remains the case that hybrid school tuition is within reach of most existing school choice policy funding levels.
In other words, we appear to be seeing more hybrid schools over time, and those schools seem to be enrolling more students, on average.
We find broad support for tightly regulated student-facing AI applications, and cautious openness to tools for teachers.
Religious observance produced the largest effects, while testing outcomes and college matriculation did not contribute meaningfully to perceived success.
The hybrid school sector remains a unique tuition market in between fulltime homeschooling/co-ops, and conventional private school options.
